title: How do you perform windowed aggregations in Flink SQL — TUMBLE(event_time, INTERVAL '1' MINUTE), HOP(event_time, INTERVAL '30' SECOND, INTERVAL '1' MINUTE), SESSION(event_time, INTERVAL '5' MINUTE), and CUMULATE — and how does the GROUP BY window TVF (Table-Valued Function) syntax work?
shortTitle: How do you perform windowed aggregations in Flink SQL

s1_definition.profdef: Windowed aggregations in Flink SQL group an unbounded stream into finite time windows and compute aggregates over each window, driven by event time and watermarks. TUMBLE produces fixed-size non-overlapping windows, HOP produces fixed-size sliding windows that overlap by a hop interval, SESSION produces gap-based windows that close after a period of inactivity, and CUMULATE produces a series of growing windows that share a start and emit early partial results up to a final size. Modern Flink SQL expresses these through windowing table-valued functions, where you call the window TVF in the FROM clause to add window_start and window_end columns and then GROUP BY those window columns together with your keys.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants to summarize transactions over time in different shapes. A TUMBLE window is like totaling transactions in back-to-back one-minute boxes that never overlap. A HOP window is like a guard who every thirty seconds totals the last full minute, so the minutes overlap. A SESSION window is like grouping a customer's burst of activity and closing the group only after they go quiet for five minutes. A CUMULATE window is like a running tally within the hour that reports the total so far every ten minutes, each report covering from the top of the hour up to now, until the hour completes. The table-valued function syntax is simply the modern way to ask Flink to stamp each transaction with which box it falls into, so you can then group and total by box.
s1_definition.oneliner: Flink SQL windows a stream with TUMBLE, HOP, SESSION, or CUMULATE via a window table-valued function in the FROM clause, then aggregates by GROUP BY window_start and window_end.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Windowed aggregations in Flink SQL group an unbounded stream into finite time windows and compute aggregates over each window, driven by event time and watermarks. TUMBLE produces fixed-size non-overlapping windows, HOP produces fixed-size sliding windows that overlap by a hop interval, SESSION produces gap-based windows that close after a period of inactivity, and CUMULATE produces a series of growing windows that share a start and emit early partial results up to a final size. Modern Flink SQL expresses these through windowing table-valued functions, where you call the window TVF in the FROM clause to add window_start and window_end columns and then GROUP BY those window columns together with your keys.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India wants to summarize transactions over time in different shapes. A TUMBLE window is like totaling transactions in back-to-back one-minute boxes that never overlap. A HOP window is like a guard who every thirty seconds totals the last full minute, so the minutes overlap. A SESSION window is like grouping a customer's burst of activity and closing the group only after they go quiet for five minutes. A CUMULATE window is like a running tally within the hour that reports the total so far every ten minutes, each report covering from the top of the hour up to now, until the hour completes. The table-valued function syntax is simply the modern way to ask Flink to stamp each transaction with which box it falls into, so you can then group and total by box.

**One line to remember:** Flink SQL windows a stream with TUMBLE, HOP, SESSION, or CUMULATE via a window table-valued function in the FROM clause, then aggregates by GROUP BY window_start and window_end.

sections.s2_technical:
The modern and recommended syntax is the windowing table-valued function. You wrap your source table in a window TVF inside the FROM clause, and Flink adds three columns to every row: window_start, window_end, and window_time. For example `FROM TABLE(TUMBLE(TABLE transactions, DESCRIPTOR(event_time), INTERVAL '1' MINUTE))` assigns each transaction to a one-minute tumbling window and exposes the window boundaries. You then write a normal GROUP BY that includes window_start and window_end alongside your grouping keys, such as `GROUP BY window_start, window_end, account_id`, and apply aggregates like COUNT, SUM, and AVG. The window TVF requires that the descriptor column, here event_time, be a time attribute with a watermark defined on the source, because event-time windows need watermarks to know when to fire.

Each window shape has its own TVF. TUMBLE takes the table, the time descriptor, and a size, giving non-overlapping windows. HOP, sometimes called sliding, takes the table, the descriptor, a slide, and a size, so `HOP(TABLE t, DESCRIPTOR(event_time), INTERVAL '30' SECOND, INTERVAL '1' MINUTE)` gives one-minute windows that advance every thirty seconds, meaning each event can belong to two windows. SESSION windows group events separated by less than a gap and merge dynamically, closing after the gap of inactivity, expressed with a session TVF and a gap interval. CUMULATE takes a step and a max size, producing windows that all start at the same point and grow by the step up to the max, emitting intermediate results, which is ideal for early dashboards like a running daily total reported every hour.

Several senior points matter. The older syntax used grouped window functions like TUMBLE_START and TUMBLE_END in the GROUP BY directly, but the window TVF approach is now preferred because it is more expressive, supports windowing joins and top-N, and cleanly exposes the window columns. A windowed aggregation generally produces an append-only result, because each window emits its result once when it closes, which means you can write it to a plain append sink, unlike an unbounded GROUP BY that produces retractions. Windows fire when the watermark passes the window end, so correct watermarking is essential; a stalled watermark means windows never fire. HOP windows with a small slide relative to the size multiply the work because each event lands in many windows, so you size them deliberately. CUMULATE is the clean way to get progressive early results without the overlap cost of HOP. And you can combine windowing with keyed grouping to get, for example, per-account per-minute totals. Mastery is knowing the TVF syntax, matching the window shape to the business question, and understanding that windowed results are append-only and watermark-driven.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India wants a per-account count and total of transactions in each fixed one-minute window for its fraud dashboard, emitted once per minute when the minute closes. This is exactly a TUMBLE windowed aggregation grouped by window and account, producing an append-only result.

Problem 2 — The bank also wants a smoother view that reports, every thirty seconds, the total over the last full minute, so the dashboard updates twice as often with overlapping windows. This is exactly a HOP window with a thirty-second slide and a one-minute size. And for a running daily total shown every few minutes, a CUMULATE window fits.

In the mini-project we build a runnable demo that reproduces the window TVF assignment and GROUP BY aggregation for TUMBLE, HOP, and CUMULATE. We define a `Txn` with an event time and amount. A `WindowTvf` computes, for a given transaction and window specification, the set of window_start and window_end pairs it belongs to, which is one pair for TUMBLE, possibly several for HOP, and a growing set for CUMULATE. A `WindowedAggregator` groups by window and account and sums amounts, firing windows whose end the watermark has passed, matching the append-only, watermark-driven behavior. A `WindowedSqlDemo` main class feeds transactions through TUMBLE, HOP, and CUMULATE assignments and prints the per-window per-account aggregates, showing how the same data yields different window shapes.

The SQL this demo models:

```sql
-- queries.sql
-- TUMBLE: fixed 1-minute windows
SELECT window_start, window_end, account_id, COUNT(*) AS cnt, SUM(amount) AS total
FROM TABLE(TUMBLE(TABLE transactions, DESCRIPTOR(event_time), INTERVAL '1' MINUTE))
GROUP BY window_start, window_end, account_id;

-- HOP: 1-minute windows sliding every 30 seconds
SELECT window_start, window_end, account_id, SUM(amount) AS total
FROM TABLE(HOP(TABLE transactions, DESCRIPTOR(event_time), INTERVAL '30' SECOND, INTERVAL '1' MINUTE))
GROUP BY window_start, window_end, account_id;

-- CUMULATE: grow every 1 min up to 5 min (early running totals)
SELECT window_start, window_end, account_id, SUM(amount) AS total
FROM TABLE(CUMULATE(TABLE transactions, DESCRIPTOR(event_time), INTERVAL '1' MINUTE, INTERVAL '5' MINUTE))
GROUP BY window_start, window_end, account_id;
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four transactions, three for Rajesh (SAV2001) at ten, fifty, and seventy seconds, and one for Priya (CUR3001) at forty seconds, processed through TUMBLE one-minute, HOP one-minute sliding thirty seconds, and CUMULATE one-minute step to five-minute max.

Step 1, TUMBLE: Each transaction gets exactly one window. Rajesh at ten and fifty seconds both floor into the window from zero to sixty, and Priya at forty seconds also falls there. Rajesh at seventy seconds falls into the window from sixty to one hundred twenty. So the zero-to-sixty window has Rajesh with count two total three hundred and Priya with count one total five hundred, while the sixty-to-one-twenty window has Rajesh with count one total three hundred.

Step 2, TUMBLE result: The aggregator emits one append-only row per window and account, exactly as a TUMBLE GROUP BY would when each window closes. There is no overlap; every transaction contributed to exactly one window.

Step 3, HOP: Each transaction can belong to multiple overlapping one-minute windows that slide every thirty seconds. Rajesh at ten seconds belongs to the window from minus thirty to thirty and the window from zero to sixty. Rajesh at fifty seconds belongs to the window from zero to sixty and the window from thirty to ninety. This overlap means the HOP output has more windows and each transaction is counted in two of them.

Step 4, HOP result: The aggregator emits more rows than TUMBLE because of the overlap, giving the smoother, more frequently updated view the dashboard wanted, at the cost of counting each event in multiple windows.

Step 5, CUMULATE: Each transaction belongs to every cumulative window, sharing the cycle start of zero, whose end is after the event, up to the five-minute max. Rajesh at ten seconds belongs to the zero-to-sixty, zero-to-one-twenty, and all larger cumulative windows up to five minutes, so the running total grows as each step window reports.

Step 6, CUMULATE result: The aggregator emits progressively larger windows that all start at zero, giving an early running total that a dashboard can show every minute without waiting for a full window to close. The demo makes the shapes concrete: TUMBLE non-overlapping, HOP overlapping, and CUMULATE growing, all from the same transactions.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Windowed aggregations in Flink SQL group an unbounded stream into finite time windows and aggregate over each, and the modern way to express them is the windowing table-valued function. You wrap your source table in a window TVF in the FROM clause, and Flink adds window_start, window_end, and window_time columns to every row, then you write an ordinary GROUP BY that includes window_start and window_end along with your keys and apply aggregates like COUNT, SUM, and AVG. There are four shapes. TUMBLE takes a size and gives fixed, non-overlapping windows, so each event lands in exactly one. HOP, also called sliding, takes a slide and a size, giving overlapping windows that advance by the slide, so an event can belong to several and you get a smoother, more frequent view at the cost of more work. SESSION groups events separated by less than a gap and closes a window after that gap of inactivity, merging dynamically. CUMULATE takes a step and a max size, producing windows that all share a start and grow by the step up to the max, which is the clean way to emit early running totals, like a daily total reported every hour.

The window TVF requires that the time descriptor column be a time attribute with a watermark defined on the source, because event-time windows fire only when the watermark passes the window end, so correct watermarking is essential or the windows never emit. A very practical point is that a windowed aggregation generally produces an append-only result, because each window emits its result once when it closes, which means you can write it to a plain append sink, unlike an unbounded GROUP BY that produces retractions. The older syntax used grouped window functions like TUMBLE_START directly in the GROUP BY, but the TVF approach is now preferred because it is more expressive and supports windowing joins and top-N. You also size HOP windows carefully, because a small slide relative to the size multiplies the per-event work, and you reach for CUMULATE when you want progressive early results without that overlap cost.

At the National Bank of India I used all of these for the fraud and reporting dashboards. A TUMBLE one-minute window gave us per-account counts and totals emitted once per minute, which was the backbone of the fraud view and conveniently append-only so it went straight to a simple sink. A HOP window of one minute sliding every thirty seconds gave the operations dashboard a smoother, twice-as-frequent view when they wanted it, and I was careful about the overlap cost. For a running daily total that leadership wanted to see updating through the day rather than only at midnight, a CUMULATE window stepping every hour up to a day was exactly right. In every case I made sure the source table had a watermark on the event-time column so the windows actually fired. Being able to write the window TVF syntax, explain the four window shapes and when each fits, note that windowed results are append-only and watermark-driven, and mention the HOP overlap cost and CUMULATE's early-result benefit, is precisely what shows genuine command of Flink SQL windowing.
